name: Bukiyip
confidence_why: Conrad and Wogiga's 1991 reference grammar states penultimate stress on virtually every word, restated by Conrad and Simatab in 1998, but Dobrin's Arapesh grammar (c. 2010) describes the Cemaun dialect of the same language with primary stress on the first or second syllable, lexically fixed or mobile on verbs, with examples that are not penultimate, and no third independent source breaks the tie.
catalog_quote: Conrad & Wogiga 1991:3: 'Penultimate word stress occurs very generally and usually coincides with high pitch on the stressed syllable. Four contrastive intonation contours have been observed. All except the imperative occur phonological clause finally.' StressTyp2 passage 741: 'Word stress is penult. (Conrad&Wogiga 1991)'
readall_conflicts: The one listed work (SIL OPD 2004) says nothing about stress, so it creates no conflict. Two other items already held by the project in the same folder (not in 'works', read only for context) do bear on the catalog's penultimate rule and disagree with each other: Conrad & Simatab 1998, Arapesh and Bukiyip comparative grammar notes (scanned page p7, Comparative Phonology item 7) states 'The basic stress pattern is the same in A as in B. There is penultimate stress with accompanying length on virtually every word.' and (p8) 'Note the sentence final falling intonation and the stress (higher pitch) on the penultimate syllable of every word.' (B = Bukiyip/Mountain Arapesh, A = Coastal Arapesh) — this agrees with the catalog. Dobrin's arapesh.org Grammar > Phonology page (lines 112-117), describing the Cemaun dialect of Mountain Arapesh, states 'Primary word stress tends to fall on either the first or second syllable. Verbs must be specified for whether they take stress on the root or on the preceding vowel, and for whether or not stress advances with the addition of object or other suffixes', with examples [nécəpokok], [nohʷánɨk], [írau Koni] vs. [iráuən] — a lexical/morphological, partly mobile pattern that contradicts a fixed: penultimate syllable characterization. So the catalog's penult (StressTyp2, presumably from Conrad & Wogiga 1991, the source Gordon's typology lists for Bukiyip) is confirmed by Conrad's own later notes but disputed by Dobrin's description of the Cemaun d…

audit.recode_to: no reclassification now. Keep penult (fixed) for Bukiyip; add a caution/contra note: Dobrin (arapesh.org phonology sketch, Cemaun coastal dialect of the same glottocode) reports primary stress on the 1st or 2nd syllable with lexically specified verb stress ([nécəpokok], [nohʷánɨkət]). If Dobrin 2001/2012 uphold this, either downgrade strict→non-strict with a dialect caution or split the coastal (Cemaun) variety from Conrad's mountain Bukiyip.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding passages are verbatim in the held Conrad & Wogiga 1991 PDF at printed p.3 (p.13) and p.124 (p.134). (2) Deciding source is the standard reference grammar (PL C-113, 297 pp, 1991), Glottolog's top entry; its stress coverage is one sentence, but a second Conrad source now obtained (Conrad & Simatab 1998 p.7-8) restates 'penultimate stress with accompanying length on virtually every word' for both mountain Bukiyip and Coastal Arapesh, and StressTyp2/Gordon 2002 rest on the same grammar. SIL OPD (2004) and Fortune 1942 (Sounds chapter) are silent. (3) The one independent description by a phonologist, Dobrin's arapesh.org grammar sketch of the Cemaun (coastal) dialect — same ISO/glottocode — contradicts: stress on 1st or 2nd syllable, lexically specified and partly mobile in verbs, with 4-syllable forms stressed initially. This is a dialect-level or analytic

sources.quote: 'Primary word stress tends to fall on either the first or second syllable. Verbs must be specified for whether they take stress on the root or on the preceding vowel, and for whether or not stress advances with the addition of object or other suffixes.
